title: Nmap
excerpt: Reliable software systems depend on foundational primitives like Nmap. Understanding how it manages state, latency, and fault tolerance separates.
author: Julian Mercer

body.text: Reliable software systems depend on foundational primitives like Nmap. Understanding how it manages state, latency, and fault tolerance separates resilient architecture from fragile code.

Nmap (Network Mapper) is a network scanner created by Gordon Lyon (also known by his pseudonym Fyodor Vaskovich). It was first released in September 1997 in Phrack magazine. Nmap is used to discover hosts and services on a computer network by sending packets and analyzing the responses.

Nmap provides a number of features for probing computer networks, including host discovery and service and operating system detection. These features are extensible by scripts that provide more advanced service detection, vulnerability detection, and other features. Nmap can adapt to network conditions including latency and congestion during a scan.
The Nmap distribution also includes the Zenmap graphical user interface, the Ncat networking utility, the Ndiff scan comparison tool and the Nping packet generation tool.

Nmap started as a Linux utility and was ported to other systems including Windows, macOS, and BSD. According to the Nmap Project, Windows, supported since 2000, has become its second most popular platform after Linux.
Features
Host discovery, Identifying hosts on a network. For example, listing the hosts that respond to TCP and/or ICMP requests or have a particular port open.

Version detection, Interrogating network services on remote devices to determine application name and version number. Nmap sends probes from its nmap-service-probes database and matches the responses against known signatures to identify the service protocol, application, version, and sometimes the device type and operating system family.
TCP/IP stack fingerprinting, Determining the operating system and hardware characteristics of network devices based on observations of network activity of said devices.

Nmap sends a series of probes and compares dozens of characteristics of the responses, such as how initial sequence numbers are generated and which TCP options are returned and in what order, against signatures developed from fingerprints submitted by users.
Scriptable interaction with the target, using Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE) and Lua programming language.
Nmap can provide further information on targets, including reverse DNS names, device types, and MAC addresses.

Nmap is distributed with several companion programs: Ncat, a reimplementation of netcat that adds support for SSL, connection redirection and proxying, Ndiff, which compares the results of two Nmap scans and reports the changes, and Nping, a tool for network packet generation, response analysis and response time measurement.
Auditing the security of a device or firewall by identifying the network connections which can be made to, or through it.
Generating traffic to hosts on a network, response analysis and response time measurement.
Academic surveys of network attack surface mapping review it among the prominent tools used for network reconnaissance.

Web-based interfaces exist that allow either controlling Nmap or analysing Nmap results from a web browser, such as IVRE.
Output

Four different output formats are offered by Nmap. Everything is saved to a file except the interactive output. Text processing software can be used to modify Nmap output, allowing the user to customize reports.

History
Nmap was first published in September 1997, as an article in Phrack Magazine with source-code included. 25 followed on 5 September 1997.

Lyon later said he had written Nmap for his own network discovery after modifying several existing port scanners to add features they lacked, and had published it in case others found it useful, the bug reports, fixes and suggestions that followed led him to continue releasing new versions.
With help and contributions of the computer security community, development continued. IPv6, SCTP) and new programs that complement Nmap's core features.
Legal issues

Nmap is a tool that can be used to discover services running on Internet connected systems. Like any computer networking tool, it could potentially be used for black hat hacking, as a precursor to attempts to gain unauthorized access to computer systems.
System administrators can use Nmap to search for unauthorized servers, or for computers that do not conform to security standards.

In 2003 Supreme Court of Finland ruled that port scanning amounted to an attempted computer break-in, which was illegal under Finnish penal code at the time:In its ruling the Supreme Court stated that the defendant had systematically carried out port scanning operations to gather information for the purpose of unauthorised break-in to the bank's computer network.
License

Nmap was originally distributed under the GNU General Public License (GPL). In later releases, Nmap's authors added clarifications and specific interpretations to the license where they felt the GPL was unclear or lacking. 50 specifically revoked the license of SCO Group to distribute Nmap software because of their views on the SCO, Linux disputes.
90, released in October 2020, Nmap is distributed under the Nmap Public Source License (NPSL), a custom license based on GPLv2 with additional terms, conditions and exceptions.

The license prohibits redistribution and use of Nmap within proprietary software and hardware products, and the Nmap Project funds its development by selling a separate Nmap OEM license to companies that embed Nmap in their products.
The project states that it believes the NPSL complies with the Open Source Definition, but it has not submitted the license for certification. 92 may also be used under the previous license terms.

The new license was questioned by several Linux distributions. 92 was not a free software license, in particular over a clause directing "proprietary software companies" to purchase a separate license.

92 was not acceptable for software it distributes, describing the clause as a field-of-endeavor restriction contrary to the Open Source Definition, and Void Linux and Debian reverted to versions released before the license change. 92, which can still be used under the earlier license terms.
Debian resumed packaging NPSL-licensed releases while discussion continued over whether the license meets the Debian Free Software Guidelines.
In popular culture

In The Matrix Reloaded, Trinity is seen using Nmap to find a host with an open SSH port, which she then compromises with a real SSH exploit to access a power plant's computer system, allowing Neo to "physically" break into a building.
The appearance of Nmap in the film was widely discussed on Internet forums and hailed as an unusually realistic example of hacking.
Nmap and NmapFE were used in The Listening, a 2006 movie about a former NSA officer who defects and mounts a clandestine counter-listening station high in the Italian alps.

Nmap source code can be seen in the movie Battle Royale, as well as brief views of the command line version of Nmap executing in Live Free or Die Hard and Bourne Ultimatum. In 2013, Nmap continued to make appearances in movies including popular sci-fi movie Elysium.

The film Dredd, a film adaptation of the famous Judge Dredd comics, was released in 2012 and also contains multiple Nmap scenes. Nmap is used for network reconnaissance and exploitation of the slum tower network. It is even seen briefly in the movie's trailer.
The command Nmap is widely used in the video game Hacknet, allowing to probe the network ports of a target system to hack it.
In Snowden, Nmap is used in the aptitude test scene about 14 minutes into the movie.
In academia

Nmap is an integral part of academic activities. It has been used for research involving the TCP/IP protocol suite and networking in general. Besides being a research tool, Nmap has also become a research topic. 7 percent detection accuracy against evasive scans on the authors' dataset.
